newsitem.title: USA: Alger Hiss was key target in communist witch-hunt era.
newsitem.headline: Alger Hiss was key target in communist witch-hunt era.

text.p: Seldom has the question of one man's guilt or innocence so troubled a nation as the Alger Hiss case did in the late 1940s and 1950s, at the start of the era of communist witch-hunts in the United States.
Was the courtly one-time State Department official and New Deal Democrat a secret Communist spy? Or was he an innocent victim of the delusions of a troubled accuser?

How one answered that question defined one's politics in the United States in the 1950s, when Sen. Joseph McCarthy spread fear and loathing in his frenzied search for those he branded "communist subversives."

But decades passed and the Hiss case faded from view to become a footnote to a troubled time. The question of his guilt or innocence never seemed to be fully answered right up to his death on Friday in New York City at the age of 92.
Hiss insisted he was innocent and sought vindication "in the court of public opinion," but his promising career came to an abrupt halt.

In contrast, his chief accuser, California Congressman Richard Nixon, progressed from his role as a member of the House Un-American Activities Committee to a vice presidential nomination and ultimately the presidency.

Hiss was the highly-paid president of the Carnegie Endowment for International Peace in 1948, when Whittaker Chambers, a rumpled, overweight journalist, said Hiss had given him U.S. government secrets to pass to the Russians.

Hiss, who studied law at Harvard and served as private secretary to Supreme Court Justice Oliver Wendell Holmes, had been one of the bright young Democrats who flocked to Washington in the 1930s to serve President Franklin Roosevelt and his New Deal administration.
A foreign policy coordinator at the State Department, he was an adviser to Roosevelt at the 1945 Yalta Conference, helped set up the United Nations and became a confidant of Supreme Court justices.
Within three years of the Chambers accusations, however, he was in prison, his career shattered and his nation divided.

Chambers, a Time magazine editor and former communist, first appeared before the House Un-American Activities Committee in August 1948 to claim Hiss was a party member from 1934 to 1938 while serving in the Roosevelt administration.
Before the year ended, Chambers added a stunning new charge -- that he was a Soviet courier and Hiss was his supplier of secrets.

It was a time of distrust in the United States. The wartime friendship with Stalin had soured into the Cold War and the United States was rent with fears that communists had infiltrated the highest levels of government.

Democratic President Harry Truman dismissed the Chambers accusations, saying they were "a red herring" to distract attention from the failure of the Republican-controlled Congress to deal with the post-war economic crisis.
Hiss sued Chambers for libel and Chambers produced classified State Department documents, some of which he said were in Hiss's handwriting and others typed on the Hiss family typewriter.
Chambers also produced microfilm of more classified U.S. documents that he kept hidden in a pumpkin on his Maryland farm. The microfilm became known as "The Pumpkin Papers."
Congressman Nixon, who took the Hiss case on as a personal "pet" project, insisted: "If the American people knew the real nature of Alger Hiss, they would boil him in oil."
Hiss could not be tried for espionage because the statute of limitations had run out on crimes allegedly committed in the 1930s. So he was charged with perjury.

At his first trial in 1949 the jury could not decide whether Hiss or Chambers was lying. A second jury, in 1950, found Hiss guilty and he was sent to jail, where he served 44 months of a five-year sentence.

In the decades that followed Hiss insisted on his innocence even as reseachers divided on the question. Ironically, Nixon's fall from power in the Watergate scandal gave Hiss great hope. Willing to believe the worst of Nixon, many came to see Hiss as his victim.
Following Watergate, Hiss asked the courts to overturn his conviction on the basis of "recently discovered" evidence. But in 1983 the Supreme Court rejected without comment his appeal for a review.

The case would continue to stir strong emotions. In 1984, a book by historian Allen Weinstein claimed Hiss had perjured himself when describing his dealings with Chambers. The author said he had started out believing Hiss was innocent but found the evidence supported the charges.
A senior adviser to Russian President Boris Yeltsin said in 1992 that newly opened files showed no evidence that Hiss had spied for Moscow.
Hiss was born on November 11, 1904, in Baltimore, Maryland, to an upper middle-class family, the elder of two sons. His hobbies were tennis, sailing and bird watching.
After his jail term he gradually made a comeback, supporting his estranged wife, Priscilla Hobson, whom he married in 1929, and their two sons by lecturing about the New Deal at universities.

In a memoir published in 1988 Hiss insisted on innocence and summed up his life this way: "I subscribe to the view that the journey travelled counts for more than the goals reached. In the words of Job, I have pursued my goals 'in mine own ways.' In that I am content."
